section_summary: This section chiefly documents international debate over arms embargoes during the Sino-Japanese conflict, especially Great Britain’s short-lived embargo on both China and Japan and U.S. reluctance to act without congressional authority. It includes diplomatic telegrams, despatches, cross-reference sheets, and press commentary from London, Geneva, Canada, China, and France, together with reports of Japanese purchases of aircraft, chemicals, metals, and surplus tractors. The papers repeatedly conclude that a nondiscriminatory embargo would disadvantage China, while an embargo against Japan alone might provoke a blockade or wider war.

subfiles.title: British warning against an embargo applying only to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the British Ambassador’s warning that a unilateral embargo against Japan could produce a blockade of Chinese ports and a general war.
subfiles.summary: The British Ambassador believes political pressure in Britain may force the government to apply its arms embargo exclusively to Japan. He and Grew agree that Japan would probably answer by blockading Chinese ports, creating a grave danger of wider war.

subfiles.title: Proposed Japanese purchase of Ethyl fluid
subfiles.about: Records informal State Department advice concerning a Japanese attempt to purchase a very large quantity of Ethyl fluid.
subfiles.summary: Francis Patterson reported that a Japanese government purchasing agent sought enough Ethyl fluid for current civilian and military consumption plus one or two years of reserves. After consulting Hornbeck, the Department informally suggested making no sale, or limiting it strictly to current needs; Patterson said his board held a similar view.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Wilson telegram 141
subfiles.about: Points to a Geneva telegram concerning Sir John Simon’s expected request for an Advisory Committee meeting on an arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Wilson’s telegram 141 from Switzerland. It identifies the subject as Simon’s expected effort to convene the Advisory Committee to discuss an arms embargo for the Far East.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on aircraft patents
subfiles.about: Points to a Western European Affairs memorandum about selling aircraft-related patents for use in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a memorandum by Green in the Division of Western European Affairs. Its subject is the sale of certain patents for Japanese use in aircraft.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Wilson telegram 142
subfiles.about: Points to Wilson’s appointment with Sir John Simon to discuss an arms embargo in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references telegram 142 from Switzerland. It notes Wilson’s appointment with Simon for discussion of the Far Eastern arms embargo.

subfiles.title: Appointment with Sir John Simon
subfiles.about: Reports that the British delegation arranged for Wilson to meet Sir John Simon about an arms embargo in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Wilson reports that the British delegation made an appointment for him to see Simon on Saturday morning. Simon had telegraphed that he wished to discuss the Far Eastern arms embargo.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch 697
subfiles.about: Points to Atherton’s despatch about the British embargo on arms for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies despatch 697 from Great Britain. The referenced document concerns Britain’s embargo on arms exports to both China and Japan.

subfiles.title: British embargo on arms for China and Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the British government’s provisional suspension of arms-export licenses to China and Japan and summarizes parliamentary and press reaction.
subfiles.summary: Britain announced that it would temporarily stop licensing arms exports to either China or Japan pending international consultation. Atherton explains that the measure could be evaded through neutral countries and was widely criticized for treating aggressor and victim alike, disadvantaging China, and sacrificing British trade without assuring international cooperation. The despatch summarizes objections by Chamberlain, Samuel, and Amery and reviews sharply divided newspaper editorials.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Phillips memorandum
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum about the British Ambassador’s inquiry into the new U.S. administration’s embargo policy.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a memorandum by Under Secretary Phillips. It concerns the British Ambassador’s request for the new administration’s policy on arms and ammunition exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to British aide-mémoire
subfiles.about: Points to a British Embassy aide-mémoire on an arms and ammunition embargo against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a statement made by the British Foreign Secretary. The statement concerned an embargo on exports of arms and ammunition to both belligerents.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to note for the British Embassy
subfiles.about: Points to a note stating that the administration would seek legislation authorizing arms-export embargoes.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a March 11 note to the British Embassy. It records the administration’s intention to press for enabling legislation concerning arms and ammunition exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Summary of French war-material sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes Paris despatch 3399 concerning French military exports and reported Japanese aircraft orders.
subfiles.summary: Official French trade returns showed no substantial war-material sales to Japan, although some private shipments had occurred. Reports of orders for French bombardment and other aircraft were unverified, while a January newspaper report was found to have recycled year-old information.

subfiles.title: Sales of war material to Japan by France
subfiles.about: Corrects an erroneous newspaper report and relays an unverified claim that Japan ordered aircraft from two French firms.
subfiles.summary: United Press correspondent Carrol said the New York Herald Tribune had confused his report with material printed more than a year earlier. French trade returns disclosed no large-scale sales, but the Financial Times reported Japanese orders for bombardment and other aircraft from two French firms. The embassy promised to seek verification.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to conversation with the Chinese Minister
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum recording Dr. Sze’s objections to Britain’s equal embargo on China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a conversation between a State Department official and the Chinese Minister. Dr. Sze expressed indignation that Britain had imposed the embargo equally upon China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Wilson telegram 145
subfiles.about: Summarizes Simon’s expectation that Britain would lift its embargo because other producing states lacked immediate authority to join it.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records Wilson’s discussion with Simon about an arms embargo in the Far East. Because many arms-producing states required new legislation, Simon believed common action would be indefinitely postponed and the British Cabinet would promptly lift its embargo.

subfiles.title: Simon anticipates lifting the British embargo
subfiles.about: Reports Simon’s view that international embargo action was impossible in the near term and Britain would probably rescind its measure.
subfiles.summary: Simon understood that the United States and several other producing states needed special legislation before they could impose embargoes. Britain alone possessed executive authority to stop shipments at its ports. He intended to report the impasse to the Cabinet and expected it to lift the embargo.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Wilson telegram 139
subfiles.about: Points to Simon’s announcement that he would consult the principal powers about an arms embargo before visiting Geneva.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references telegram 139 from Wilson. It concerns Simon’s statement in the House of Commons that he planned to contact the principal powers about a Far Eastern embargo.

subfiles.title: Simon’s planned consultations on an arms embargo
subfiles.about: Requests information about any Departmental exchange of views with Simon before Simon’s arrival in Geneva.
subfiles.summary: Wilson reports press accounts that Simon intended to consult the principal powers about an arms embargo before coming to Geneva. He asks to be informed of any exchanges with Simon so that he can be guided in later discussions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Wilson telegram 149
subfiles.about: Points to Simon’s warning about the likely effects of an embargo imposed only upon Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references Wilson’s telegram 149. Simon believed a Japan-only embargo would probably prevent arms from reaching China and create grave complications.

subfiles.title: Consequences of an embargo against Japan alone
subfiles.about: Relays Simon’s emphatic warning that a unilateral embargo against Japan could stop Chinese imports and provoke grave complications.
subfiles.summary: At the Department’s suggestion, Wilson informally asked Simon about an embargo applying only to Japan. Simon replied that such a measure could prevent any arms from reaching China and would risk the gravest complications with Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Department telegram 85
subfiles.about: Points to instructions explaining the administration’s position on arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references Department telegram 85 to Switzerland. Its subject is the administration’s attitude and policy toward exports of arms and ammunition to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: U.S. position on Far Eastern arms embargoes
subfiles.about: Explains the absence of executive embargo authority and instructs Wilson how to discuss proposed embargoes with Simon, Ruspoli, and Drummond.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that the president cannot impose an arms embargo without congressional legislation, although the administration intends to seek that authority. It considers an immediate equal embargo on China and Japan unhelpful and warns that a Japan-only embargo could lead Japan to block Chinese deliveries and provoke conflict with other powers. Wilson may convey these views informally but must emphasize that the United States cannot presently join embargoes in Asia or Latin America.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram 89
subfiles.about: Points to instructions that the American representative avoid participation in Far Eastern arms-export discussions.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram instructed the representative in Switzerland not to participate in conversations examining arms exports and the Far Eastern situation. The sheet files that instruction under the Japan arms subject.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Canadian despatch 1282
subfiles.about: Points to Boal’s report on Canadian press reactions to the British arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies despatch 1282 from Canada. It notes that Canadian newspapers initially greeted Britain’s embargo on exports to China and Japan with extreme enthusiasm.

subfiles.title: British arms embargo and the Far East
subfiles.about: Reviews the Canadian press’s changing response to Britain’s imposition and withdrawal of the arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: Canadian enthusiasm diminished after newspapers recognized that existing contracts were exempt, China would suffer more than Japan, and British neutrality conflicted with acceptance of the Lytton Report. The Montreal Gazette suggested the policy reflected Britain’s traditional friendship with Japan, while the Toronto Mail and Empire continued to praise Britain after the embargo was lifted. Roosevelt’s plan to seek general embargo authority received approval, though some writers faulted Washington for not acting sooner.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hackworth memorandum
subfiles.about: Points to a Legal Adviser’s memorandum on precedents for prohibiting arms exports to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references Hackworth’s response to an inquiry from Senator Borah’s office. The inquiry sought precedents for Senator Dill’s January 26, 1932 joint resolution concerning arms exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hornbeck memorandum on embargo legislation
subfiles.about: Points to Hornbeck’s view that the executive branch should not urge Congress to authorize a Far Eastern arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. Hornbeck argued against executive advocacy of legislation empowering the president to impose an embargo on Far Eastern arms exports.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Barnard C. Inman letter
subfiles.about: Points to a letter arguing that an embargo against Japan alone would not prevent Japanese acquisition of war matériel.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a letter from Barnard C. Inman. Inman believed Japan would capture war matériel sent to other countries, rendering a Japan-only embargo ineffective.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on reported strategic shipments
subfiles.about: Introduces a military report about shipments of chemicals and barbed wire apparently destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note describes the attached military information as concerning caustic soda, soda ash, barbed wire, and toluol. The goods reportedly left an American port for eventual delivery to Japan.

subfiles.title: Possible G-2 information on shipments to Japan
subfiles.to: Chief of Staff, United States Army
subfiles.about: Reports unusually large shipments of chemical precursors and barbed wire allegedly routed through South America to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A chemical-industry source reported roughly sixty carloads of caustic soda and soda ash plus several carloads of barbed wire being loaded at Pier 98, South Wharves. The source also described a large shipment of toluol from the same port. The report notes that the alkalis could be used in smokeless powder and toluol in TNT manufacture.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about exporting surplus tractors to Japan
subfiles.from: T. H. Fowler, Valley Forge Steel & Tool Company
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Department would license the export to Japan of surplus tractors obtained from the Caterpillar Tractor Company.
subfiles.summary: The company had purchased twenty-five ten-ton and twenty-five five-ton tractors formerly held at Raritan Arsenal. Before negotiating a sale to the Japanese government, Fowler requested an expedited ruling on whether an export license would be issued.

subfiles.title: Conversation concerning surplus tractors
subfiles.about: Records War Department information on the condition and prior disposal of tractors proposed for sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Major Gruber said the War Department had transferred the tractors to Caterpillar without restrictions on their future use. The Department considered them junk that might run only briefly after repair, with their principal value lying in salvageable parts.

subfiles.title: Reply on export license for tractors
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Advises that no license was required for exporting arms and munitions of war to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Fowler’s inquiry about the contemplated sale of surplus tractors to the Japanese government. It states that no export license was necessary, even for articles classed as arms or munitions of war.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hornbeck memorandum on a British inquiry
subfiles.about: Points to a suggested response that the United States lacked authority to impose a Far Eastern arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a Hornbeck memorandum anticipating an inquiry from the British government. Hornbeck proposed replying that the Department had no legal authority to impose the contemplated embargo.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Atherton despatch 744
subfiles.about: Points to Atherton’s report that Britain lifted its embargo on arms for Japan on March 13.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies despatch 744 from Great Britain. It records the termination of Britain’s embargo on arms for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: British embargo on arms for China and Japan lifted
subfiles.about: Reports Britain’s March 13 cancellation of its provisional arms embargo and the domestic response.
subfiles.summary: Stanley Baldwin told the House of Commons that Britain was ending its embargo because international agreement was not foreseeable and unilateral action was useless. The government nevertheless intended to pursue negotiations for future uniform action. Atherton notes that the reversal caused little surprise after widespread criticism of the original policy.

subfiles.title: French aircraft orders for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports confirmation that Japan had placed aircraft orders with Breguet and Potez, although the military attaché had not yet verified the information.
subfiles.summary: Carrol of the United Press said a member of Matsuoka’s staff confirmed the report of Japanese aircraft purchases while passing through Paris. He identified the firms as Breguet and Potez. The embassy’s military attaché had not yet independently verified the story.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Wilson telegram 159
subfiles.about: Points to Wilson’s report that arms-producing states awaited the U.S. position before deciding on an embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references telegram 159 from Switzerland. It says producing states were reluctant to take an embargo position until the United States clarified its attitude.

subfiles.title: U.S. influence over international embargo decisions
subfiles.about: Warns that other arms-producing states will probably make their embargo decisions contingent upon U.S. policy.
subfiles.summary: Wilson observes that committee members repeatedly subordinated their positions to those of other states and awaited U.S. enabling legislation. He believes American decisions on Peru or Japan would largely determine whether other producing countries joined an embargo. Because Britain feared action against Japan while France might support it, he recommends prior consultations with Britain, France, and Italy before the United States announces a position.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to proposed Chinese appeal for an embargo
subfiles.about: Points to a Hornbeck memorandum concerning a Chinese request for an arms embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum. It concerns an anticipated effort by the Chinese Minister to urge an embargo on arms exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Department telegram 92
subfiles.about: Points to instructions that the United States avoid discussion of its attitude toward a proposed embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references telegram 92 to Switzerland. The Department did not wish to be drawn into discussion of the American position on any proposed embargo against Japan.

subfiles.title: Wilson disclaims urging U.S. responsibility
subfiles.about: Agrees that the United States should not accept responsibility for an embargo decision belonging to the League of Nations.
subfiles.summary: Wilson fully agrees that the United States should avoid responsibility for a decision properly resting with the League. He explains that his earlier telegrams were intended only to warn how the situation was developing at Geneva.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hornbeck review of British approaches
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum outlining British efforts to obtain U.S. views on a Far Eastern arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references a Hornbeck memorandum in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. It outlines the British government’s request for American views and the action taken in response.

subfiles.title: Summary of revised assessment of French aircraft orders
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Paris report concluding that Japanese orders from Breguet and Potez were routine and not substantial.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to Paris despatch 3445 and its earlier report of substantial Japanese aircraft purchases. After investigation, the military attaché concluded that the orders were neither important nor unusual.

subfiles.title: Verification of Japanese aircraft orders in France
subfiles.about: Corrects the earlier impression that Japanese aircraft orders from Breguet and Potez were substantial.
subfiles.summary: The military attaché verified that Japan had placed orders with Breguet and Potez. His sources denied that the orders were substantial or important and described them as normal commercial activity. The attaché accepted that assessment.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about selling scrap steel and iron to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether there is any objection to negotiating the sale of scrap steel and iron to the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Barry seeks advice before approaching Japan’s purchasing agent. He proposes selling the Japanese government an unspecified quantity of scrap steel and iron.

subfiles.title: Reply on sale of scrap metal to Japan
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: States that the Department knew of no legal prohibition against selling scrap steel and iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department answers Barry’s April 4 inquiry about scrap metal. It advises that, so far as it is aware, no law prohibited the proposed sale to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Johnson despatch 2002
subfiles.about: Points to editorials from Peiping and Tientsin about Britain’s supposedly impartial arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Johnson’s despatch 2002 from China. The enclosed editorials discussed Britain’s equal embargo against China and Japan and were accompanied by the minister’s comments.

subfiles.title: Editorials on the arms embargo
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, U.S. Legation Peiping
subfiles.about: Forwards Chinese newspaper editorials and evaluates the likely consequences of alternative arms embargoes.
subfiles.summary: The editorials argue that a meaningful embargo should target the covenant-breaking state but acknowledge that practical considerations complicate such action. They warn that a Japan-only embargo could produce a blockade of Chinese ports and a major international crisis. Johnson concludes that an embargo against both states would injure China, while one against Japan alone could worsen the wider problem.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Cunningham despatch 8818
subfiles.about: Points to a Shanghai despatch on Britain’s arms embargo and its subsequent withdrawal.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a despatch by Cunningham from Shanghai. Its subject is the British embargo against China and Japan and the measure’s cancellation.

subfiles.title: British arms embargo against China and Japan and its withdrawal
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Cunningham, American Consulate General Shanghai
subfiles.about: Forwards Shanghai editorials on the British embargo and comments on the broader problem of arms entering China.
subfiles.summary: Cunningham transmits Chinese- and English-language editorials arguing that an equal embargo would weaken China while doing little to restrain Japan unless other producing states joined Britain. Although the embargo had already been canceled, he considered the commentary of some interest. He adds that arms imports into China also facilitated banditry because discharged soldiers retained weapons and irregular groups could readily obtain arms and munitions.

subfiles.title: The Arms Embargo
subfiles.about: Argues that Britain’s isolated embargo was impractical but that Simon’s position should not be interpreted as approval of Japanese action.
subfiles.summary: The editorial maintains that no embargo could work without simultaneous action by the major powers and that the League of Nations remained the proper mechanism for concerted pressure. It describes Britain’s equal embargo as likely to antagonize both belligerents without stopping the Jehol campaign. While acknowledging that Japan had violated the League Covenant, it defends Simon’s view that Jehol formed part of the broader and unusually complex Manchurian dispute.

subfiles.title: British Arms Embargo
subfiles.about: Condemns Britain’s equal embargo as a violation of its League obligations and as discrimination against China.
subfiles.summary: The editorial argues that China was resisting aggression and therefore deserved support under Article XVI of the League Covenant. It says Britain continued supplying Japan with iron and ore from British India and British Malaya while withholding finished arms from China. The policy is characterized as an evasion of Britain’s obligations and an advantage to Japanese munitions production.

subfiles.title: Sin Wan Pao editorial on the British arms embargo
subfiles.about: Argues that equal treatment of China and Japan disregarded the League Covenant and materially weakened Chinese resistance.
subfiles.summary: The editorial asks whether Britain regarded Japan’s invasion of Jehol as war and argues that League obligations displaced ordinary neutrality. It criticizes Simon’s refusal to discriminate between the aggressor and China, asserting that Britain’s embargo would not materially weaken Japan but would reduce China’s ability to resist. It suggests that restricting raw materials for Japanese munitions production would have had greater effect.
